subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how data was shared so freely [Thinking]
passage:
Rajni, you asked what changed my habits, and it wasn't the breach itself. It was the question I asked afterwards: why did six different services already hold my name, my number and my birthday? Nobody forced me. I just typed it all in, every time, because the form had boxes.

So I traced it back. Most of those boxes were optional. I never read the permission screens either, I just pressed accept. That was the real root of it.

Now I give the minimum, and I skip optional fields. I made a separate email address only for sign-ups. And I read what an app asks for before saying yes, even if it takes a minute. I'm Tarun, and I've deleted four accounts I didn't need.

qa.q: What did Tarun make for sign-ups?
qa.a: A separate email address only for sign-ups.

qa.q: What might Tarun have been feeling when tracing the six services back to habit?
qa.a: Tarun was probably uneasy and a little embarrassed at having shared so freely, since habit and not any need was the real cause.

qa.q: What could Tarun do next to keep the new habit from slipping, and why?
qa.a: Tarun could check once a season which accounts still hold personal details and remove the ones not used, because habits need a regular reminder.

qa.q: How might Rajni, who asked the question, see Tarun's answer?
qa.a: Rajni may notice that Tarun blames the habit instead of the breach, which makes the answer useful to anyone who hears it.

grounding: Asking why so many services held the same details, the person decides to give minimum data, use a separate sign-up email and read permissions.

subtype: Approach: root-cause thinking about how data was shared so freely [Thinking]
passage: I'm Divyansh, and I share a study table in the hostel library with Kavitha, so I watched the whole thing. On Tuesday she got a notice that a ticket-booking site had leaked her name, phone number and birthday. Instead of only changing the password, she opened a notebook and started talking to herself. "Why does a ticket site need my birthday? Why does the gym app have my home address?" She listed eleven services and ticked the ones holding the same details. Nine of them. "So the problem isn't this one leak. It's that I hand everything to everyone." By evening she had made a second email address just for sign-ups and was going through app permissions, switching off contacts and location one by one. I can't say whether she was scared or just annoyed, but she didn't stop until the list was done.

qa.q: How many of the services on Kavitha's list held the same details?
qa.a: Nine of the eleven services she listed held the same details.

qa.q: What does Kavitha's question about the ticket site suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems uneasy and irritated; asking why a ticket site needs her birthday shows she is suspicious of how much she has been handing over.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha add to her plan, and why?
qa.a: She could close the accounts she no longer uses, because an old account she has forgotten still holds the same details and can leak again.

qa.q: How does the evening look to Divyansh, who only watched?
qa.a: Divyansh sees steady, careful work but cannot tell if Kavitha was scared or annoyed, only that she kept going until the list was finished.

grounding: Shows the person tracing why so many services held the same details and changing habits with a separate sign-up email and a check of permissions.

passage:
Monday. The email said a college-fest registration site had been breached. By night Manoj had four calls about loans he never asked for. He blocked each number and lay awake feeling sick.
Thursday. His cousin Hansa found him scrolling through old sign-ups. "What are you hunting for?"
"Why did a fest pass need my home address and both my parents' numbers? I filled every box just because it was there." He counted aloud: the fest, two shopping sites, a quiz app, all holding the same phone number and address. "If I stop giving extra, there's less to leak."
Three weeks later. A coding-contest form asked for his address. It was marked optional, so he skipped it, used his new sign-up-only email, and tapped Deny when the app wanted his contacts. Hansa grinned; she had been nagging him about this for months.

qa.q: What did the fest pass ask for that made Manoj question it?
qa.a: It asked for his home address and both his parents' numbers.

qa.q: How was Manoj feeling on Monday night, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was shaken and uneasy; after four calls about loans he never asked for, he blocked the numbers and lay awake feeling sick.

qa.q: What else could Manoj try besides skipping optional boxes?
qa.a: He could delete accounts he no longer uses, like the quiz app, so fewer places keep his phone number and address.

qa.q: How might Hansa see the change in Manoj over the three weeks?
qa.a: Hansa sees him move from sleepless worry to calmly tapping Deny on a contacts request, which looks like the habit she kept nagging about has finally stuck.

grounding: Shows the person asking why every service held the same details, then giving less data, using a separate sign-up email and refusing permissions.
